blocks.text: Meanwhile, that there are some serpents which cannot be charmed seems deducible even from Scripture. For in Ierem. VIII, 17. God threatens that he will send among the Israelites [III, 171] נחשים צפעונים אשר אין להם לחש, serpents, reguli, against which there is no charm. The Complutensian edition has οἷς οὐκ ἔστιν ἐκσπᾶσαι [hois ouk estin ekspasai], from which one cannot tear oneself away; but others better, οἷς οὐκ ἔστιν ἐπάσαι [hois ouk estin epasai], which one cannot charm. And in Eccles. X, 11. Solomon says that a בעל לשון, a slanderer, is no better (that is, just as pernicious) than אם נשך הנחש בלא לחש, if a serpent bites without charm, that is, uncharmed, or one that cannot be charmed. And in the passage of the Psalmist with which we are concerned, the deaf asp is said to stop its ear, so as not to hear the voice of the charmer. Indeed, a serpent is thought to resist a charm in two ways: either when it sings back, or when it grows deaf to the song. Recanere [to sing back], ἀντᾴδειν [antadein], or recantare if you prefer, is to repel and turn back the charm by a contrary hissing. Pliny, book 28, ch. 2: Not a few (believe) that the serpents themselves sing back, [col. 391] (so I read with Turnebus ^{b)}), and that this is the only understanding they have. Aristotle, of the Thessalian witch: Εἶτα μιμεῖσθαι τὴν φωνὴν τοῦ θηρίου· τὸ δὲ ἀντᾴδειν, καὶ προσιέναι· [Eita mimeisthai tēn phōnēn tou thēriou; to de antadein, kai prosienai;] Then (the witch began) to imitate the voice of the serpent; but the serpent sang back and approached. A serpent against which the charm is ineffective, because it sings against the song in this way, is called صل [ṣil] sil in Arabic, as one that is not affected by the song is called اصم [aṣamm] asammo, that is, deaf. Properly صل [ṣil] sil is a ringing or shrill serpent, that is, one which, uttering a certain shrill sound, sings and hisses against the magician. But by a phrase as familiar to the Hebrews and Arabs as it is unknown to the Greeks and Romans, a serpent is said to grow deaf to the song, or, what is the same, to stop its ear, when it is no more affected by the song than if it were deaf or had its ears stopped. So Kimchi took it in the passage of the Psalm, where he says of the asp: זה הנחש הקשה לא יועיל בו לחש כאילו הוא חרש וכאילו יאטם אזנו שלו ישמע מה שלוחשים לו, That serpent is hard, against which a charm avails no more than if it were deaf, or hardened its ear, so as not to hear the songs with which they charm it. By the same phrase, one who is hard and merciless toward the poor is said to harden his ear to the cry of the poor, Prov. XXI, 13. And the pious man stops his ear, lest he hear of bloodshed, Es. XXXIII, 15., that is, he is so averse to cruel and bloodthirsty counsels, and attends to them no more when they are proposed by the wicked, than if he had his ears stopped. So also when it is said of Aeneas in book 4 of the Aeneid,
— — — but he is moved by no weeping, nor does he listen yielding to any words. The Fates stand in the way, and a god blocks the man's gentle ears.

That is, he made him as unbending to the prayers of Dido and Anna as if he had blocked his ears. In like manner the asp is deaf to the song and stops its ear when the song has as little power over it as if it were entirely deaf and had stopped its ears. The antecedent stands for the consequent. [III, 172] Nor, I think, is it taken otherwise by Avicenna when he so often repeats that this or that serpent is of the kind of the deaf, as is shown more fully below.

Furthermore, whether the serpent sings back or grows deaf to the song, it is believed not only to escape, but also to create danger for the magician. So in Aristotle, when the sacred serpent sang against the Thessalian sorceress, she very nearly sank into a deadly sleep. And, as Alcimus testifies in the place cited above,
Sometimes the charmer perishes, if the deaf serpent has scorned the cunning murmurs of the adjurer.

Either the whole force of the charm, by the just judgment of God, turns to the destruction of its author, or the serpent inflicts a lethal wound on the charmer. To this belongs the celebrated example ^{c)} of that magician of Salzburg who, when he was striving to drive all the serpents within one mile into a certain pit, was at last killed by a single huge and aged one that leapt upon him. Accordingly the Son of Sirach teaches that magicians too are bitten by serpents, in these words of Ecclesiasticus, chapter 12, verse 13: Τίς ἐλεήσει ἐπαοιδὸν ὀφιόδηκτον, καὶ πάντας τοὺς προσάγοντας θηρίοις; [Tis eleēsei epaoidon ophiodēkton, kai pantas tous prosagontas thēriois?] Who will pity a charmer bitten by a serpent, or any of those who go near venomous beasts? For there θηρία [thēria] signifies not any wild beasts whatever, but venomous ones, as we have already proved earlier ^{d)}.
